concept.name: Model Serving & GPU Batching

relationships.description: Connects Model Serving & GPU Batching to llm prompt engineering in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Group concurrent inference requests into tensor batches on the GPU to shift workloads from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound without blowing tail latency.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use dynamic batching with a tight queue timeout (2–10 ms) for fixed-shape encoders, and iteration-level continuous batching with PagedAttention for autoregressive LLMs.

concept.whyItMatters: Serving models at batch size 1 leaves modern GPUs (like NVIDIA A100/H100) 80–90% idle because loading model weights from HBM into SRAM dominates compute time. Intelligent batching multiplies throughput 5–20x per GPU while keeping p99 latency within strict interactive SLOs.
whenToUse: High-concurrency GPU inference (encoders, vision models, embeddings, or LLMs) where single-request execution is HBM memory-bandwidth bound.
Traffic arrives asynchronously from many concurrent users (e.g., >20 RPS) so requests naturally overlap within a 2–15 ms window.
GPU infrastructure dominates unit economics and maximizing tokens-per-second or inferences-per-dollar is a primary goal.
whenNotToUse: Ultra-low-traffic endpoints (<2 RPS) where waiting for a batch window adds pure latency with zero batch formation.
Strict single-request hard real-time loops (<5 ms total budget) where any queuing delay is unacceptable.
Tiny CPU-bound models (e.g., logistic regression, small GBDTs) where per-sample inference already takes <200 microseconds.
keyPoints: Batching amortizes HBM weight reads across $B$ inputs, raising arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte) toward the GPU's roofline.
Dynamic batching (Triton Inference Server) buffers incoming requests up to `max_batch_size` or `max_queue_delay_microseconds` (typically 2,000–10,000 us).
Static padding wastes compute on variable-length sequences; bucket by sequence length or use ragged/packed tensors.

Autoregressive LLMs fail under request-level batching because short prompts wait behind long generations; continuous (iteration-level) batching (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) swaps finished sequences out after every decode step.
PagedAttention eliminates KV-cache fragmentation by storing attention keys/values in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks (e.g., 16 tokens/block), increasing effective batch size 2–4x.

examples.title: Triton Dynamic Batching for Dense Embeddings
examples.scenario: A semantic search service running a 330M-parameter BGE embedding model on an NVIDIA L4 GPU at batch=1 capped out at 140 RPS with 18% GPU utilization.
examples.outcome: Enabling Triton dynamic batching (`max_batch_size: 32`, `max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000`) raised throughput to 1,180 RPS (8.4x) while keeping p99 latency at 21 ms.

examples.title: vLLM Continuous Batching for 70B LLM Chat
examples.scenario: Request-level static batching on Llama-3-70B forced 50-token replies to wait 12 seconds for a 1,500-token code generation in the same batch.
examples.outcome: Switching to vLLM with iteration-level continuous batching and PagedAttention cut p99 Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) from 2.4 s to 190 ms and boosted decode throughput from 180 to 940 tokens/s.

tradeOffs.pro: Larger queue windows (e.g., 20 ms) form fuller batches and maximize GPU utilization.
tradeOffs.con: Every millisecond in the queue adds directly to p99 latency, especially during off-peak traffic.

tradeOffs.pro: Request-level batching is trivial to implement in Triton/TorchServe for fixed-length vision or encoder models.
tradeOffs.con: Continuous batching is mandatory for variable-length LLM decoding to avoid head-of-line blocking, at the cost of complex KV-cache block management.

tradeOffs.factor: Large Batch Size vs. VRAM Headroom (OOM Risk)
tradeOffs.pro: Larger batches (64–256) push compute utilization near saturation.
tradeOffs.con: Activation memory and KV-cache grow linearly with batch size and sequence length, risking sudden CUDA OOM crashes on long-prompt bursts.

failureModes.name: Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking in Static LLM Batches
failureModes.description: One 4,096-token generation stalls 15 already-finished 64-token requests in the same batch, spiking p99 latency 10x.
failureModes.mitigation: Use iteration-level continuous batching (vLLM / TensorRT-LLM) so completed sequences eject immediately after emitting EOS.

failureModes.name: Prefill-Decode Interference
failureModes.description: A massive 16k-token prompt prefill hogs GPU SMs for 400 ms, causing visible stuttering (ITL > 200 ms) for all streaming decode users.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable chunked prefill (splitting long prefills into 512-token chunks) or disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools.

failureModes.name: KV-Cache OOM & Preemption Thrash
failureModes.description: Too many concurrent requests exhaust GPU VRAM for KV-cache, forcing the scheduler to preempt and recompute sequences repeatedly.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap `max_num_seqs` and `gpu_memory_utilization` (e.g., 0.90), use FP8 KV-cache quantization, and return HTTP 429 when queue depth exceeds SLO.

failureModes.name: Low-Traffic Queue Penalty
failureModes.description: At 1 AM with 2 RPS, every single request sits idle for the full `max_queue_delay` (e.g., 15 ms) waiting for a second request that never arrives.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep `max_queue_delay_microseconds` tight (2–5 ms) or use adaptive batching that dispatches immediately when concurrency is low.

commonMistakes: Tuning `max_batch_size` without setting a bounded `max_queue_delay_microseconds`, causing unbounded tail latency.
Padding every sequence in a batch to `max_seq_len` (e.g., 4,096) instead of padding only to the longest sequence in that batch.
Running Python/FastAPI tokenization synchronously on the same event loop as GPU dispatch, starving the batcher.
Measuring only average throughput while ignoring Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Inter-Token Latency (ITL) p99.
Deploying without admission control/backpressure, allowing unbounded queues to trigger client timeouts on already-stale requests.

sections.content:
## The idea

GPU inference at batch size 1 is overwhelmingly **memory-bandwidth bound**: streaming 140 GB of FP16 weights from HBM to compute cores for a single token wastes ~85% of the chip's Tensor Core FLOPs. **Model serving batching** coalesces concurrent requests into a single matrix-matrix operation (`GEMM`) so weights are read once from HBM and reused across $B$ inputs. For fixed-latency encoders, **dynamic batching** trades a bounded 2–10 ms queue wait for massive throughput gains; for autoregressive LLMs, **continuous batching** schedules at the single-token iteration boundary so requests enter and exit without waiting for peers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a continuous-batching LLM server (**vLLM** with **PagedAttention**) serving Llama-3-8B on an A100-80GB:

1. **Async Tokenization & Ingress**: Clients send gRPC/HTTP SSE requests. A Rust/C++ tokenizer pool converts text to token IDs off the GPU thread and pushes them into the scheduler queue.
2. **Iteration-Level Scheduling**: At the start of every 25 ms decode step, the scheduler checks free 16-token KV-cache blocks in VRAM. It admits waiting requests (prefill chunks of 512 tokens) alongside active decode sequences up to `max_num_batched_tokens=2048`.
3. **PagedAttention Forward Pass**: A single fused CUDA kernel computes attention across non-contiguous KV-cache blocks for all $B$ active sequences simultaneously.
4. **Immediate Ejection & Streaming**: Any sequence emitting `<eos>` frees its KV-cache blocks immediately and closes its SSE stream; remaining sequences advance to the next step while a new queued request takes the freed slot.

sections.content:
## Latency-throughput physics

Understanding the GPU **roofline model** explains why batching works and where it stops scaling:

- **Memory-Bound Regime ($B < B_{\text{ridge}}$)**: For FP16 matrix multiplication on an H100 (3.35 TB/s HBM, 989 TFLOPS FP16), the ridge point is $\approx 295$ FLOPs/byte. Below batch size ~128–256 for decode, doubling batch size $B$ nearly doubles throughput with almost zero increase in step latency.
- **Compute-Bound Regime ($B \ge B_{\text{ridge}}$)**: Once arithmetic intensity saturates Tensor Cores, increasing $B$ further yields flat throughput while step latency grows linearly with $B$.

## Batching strategies compared

| Strategy | Scheduling Granularity | Padding Overhead | HoL Blocking | Ideal Workload |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Static Batching** | Fixed batch size $B$ | High (pad to max len) | Severe | Offline bulk scoring |
| **Dynamic Batching** | Request-level + queue timeout | Medium (pad to batch max) | Moderate on variable len | Vision, embeddings, encoders (Triton) |
| **Continuous Batching** | Token-iteration level | Near zero (ragged/PagedKV) | Eliminated | Autoregressive LLMs (vLLM, TRT-LLM) |
| **Chunked Prefill** | Fixed token budget/step | Near zero | Eliminates prefill stalls | Mixed long-context + interactive chat |

## Failure modes

Watch for three production failure modes as traffic scales:

- **Queue Buildup Beyond Client Timeout**: If arrival rate $\lambda$ exceeds service rate $\mu$ for 30 seconds, the batcher processes requests whose clients already timed out at 5 seconds.
- **Dynamic Shape Recompilation**: Frameworks like `torch.compile` or TensorRT without wildcard shape profiles trigger multi-second JIT stalls whenever a new batch size appears.
- **Cross-Request Memory Leaks**: Improperly detached tensors or unfreed KV-cache blocks slowly shrink available VRAM until the pod OOMs.

## Production hardening

Protect interactive SLOs under bursty load:

- **Admission Control**: Reject requests with HTTP 429 (`Retry-After`) when estimated queue wait exceeds 50% of the TTFT SLO.
- **Warmup Profiles**: Pre-compile TensorRT engines or run dummy warmup batches for powers-of-two batch sizes `[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]` before marking Kubernetes readiness probes healthy.
- **Prefix Caching**: Enable automatic radix/prefix KV-cache sharing (e.g., SGLang RadixAttention or vLLM APC) when requests share long system prompts.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Measure baseline batch=1 vs. batch=16 latency and throughput to locate your GPU roofline.
- [ ] Set `max_queue_delay_microseconds` between 2,000 and 10,000 us for dynamic batching.
- [ ] Use continuous batching + PagedAttention + chunked prefill for all LLM deployments.
- [ ] Pre-warm all batch-size shapes during container startup before readiness passes.
- [ ] Enforce queue-depth admission control (HTTP 429) and track TTFT/ITL p99 separately.

interviewProblems.title: Model Serving & GPU Batching
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Model Serving & GPU Batching. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Group concurrent inference requests into tensor batches on the GPU to shift workloads from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound without blowing tail latency.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: GPU Engine + PagedKV applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Token Streamer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Token Streamer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use iteration-level continuous batching (vLLM / TensorRT-LLM) so completed sequences eject immediately after emitting EOS.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use dynamic batching with a tight queue timeout (2–10 ms) for fixed-shape encoders, and iteration-level continuous batching with PagedAttention for autoregressive LLMs.
Avoid trap: Tuning `max_batch_size` without setting a bounded `max_queue_delay_microseconds`, causing unbounded tail latency.
Avoid trap: Padding every sequence in a batch to `max_seq_len` (e.g., 4,096) instead of padding only to the longest sequence in that batch.
When to reach for it: High-concurrency GPU inference (encoders, vision models, embeddings, or LLMs) where single-request execution is HBM memory-bandwidth bound.
When to reach for it: Traffic arrives asynchronously from many concurrent users (e.g., >20 RPS) so requests naturally overlap within a 2–15 ms window.

putItTogether.title: Putting Model Serving Batching Together
putItTogether.summary: Use dynamic batching with a tight queue timeout (2–10 ms) for fixed-shape encoders, and iteration-level continuous batching with PagedAttention for autoregressive LLMs.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Model Serving Batching before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Enabling Triton dynamic batching (`max_batch_size: 32`, `max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000`) raised throughput to 1,180 RPS (8.4x) while keeping p99 latency at 21 ms.
